title: Mars will need cowboys, not committees
text:
In 1886, Friedrich Nietzsche published Beyond Good and Evil. One hundred and forty years later, the book still asks its original question: what happens when inherited moral maps lose their force, and human beings must create values from strength rather than receive them. The anniversary is worth marking for a second reason. At the same historical moment, on the other side of the Atlantic, a short-lived American experiment was already living out a practical version of that challenge. This is synchronicity, not cause and effect. The cowboys and lawmen of the 1870s and 1880s were not reading German philosophy. They simply operated under conditions that made the underlying drive visible.

Nietzsche diagnosed a Europe still clinging to categories of good and evil that no longer rested on living power. He called for a higher type capable of standing beyond those categories and imposing new ones. In the American West, a different response was taking shape. The classic open-range cowboy was not an ancient archetype. He was a late 19-century invention — an improvisation that combined Mexican vaquero technique with post-Civil War commercial cattle drives across a temporary ecological niche created by the destruction of the buffalo and the defeat of the Plains tribes. For roughly two decades this produced a working culture governed more by reputation, the brand, and calculated interest than by distant statute or inherited duty. A man chose his loyalties according to who paid, who protected, and who offered the better chance of survival. Those loyalties could be fierce while they lasted. They were also provisional.
